Your neatHack team is ready — setup guide & credits
Inbox

neatHack by neatlogs <ajay@events.neatlogs.com>
1:28 PM (1 minute ago)
to me

Hi Sathwik Giddi,

Your team um has completed web check-in. You’re ready to build!

As team leader, you receive the setup and credits instructions for your team. Credits are allocated once per team, not per member.

Join the neatHack Discord
Join our Discord for event announcements, help with setup and credits, and support from organisers and mentors.

https://neatlogs.com/discord

1. Build with neatlogs — free throughout the hackathon
All neatlogs paid plans are available to you for free for the duration of neatHack. We believe no good idea should be held back by a paywall.

Sign up at https://app.neatlogs.com and create your project.

Start with our step-by-step setup guide, with screenshots, a ready-to-use coding-agent prompt, and troubleshooting: https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/neatlogs-setup-guide.html

For framework-specific instructions, see https://docs.neatlogs.com.

Run your agent and verify that its traces appear in the dashboard. Use those traces to investigate failures and verify your fixes.

2. Set up Entire
Follow the Entire guide for neatHack: https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/

Connect your GitHub repository, install the CLI, and capture your first checkpoint.

Explore Trails and optional Graph/Brain features. Include an accessible checkpoint link and ID in your submission.

3. Access cfo.ai paid plans for free
Use the dedicated neatHack signup link to access any cfo.ai paid plan for free: https://cfo.ai/neathacks

A card is required during signup. Immediately after signing up, cancel your subscription in Settings → Billing. You won’t be billed if you cancel immediately.

The neatHack team will provide your cfo.ai credits directly.

Use cfo.ai to plan your agent’s pricing, costs, revenue, and runway. Include the resulting business plan in your submission.

4. Claim your Crustdata credits
Get 5,000 Crustdata credits to build with company and people data.

Use promo code: NEATLOGS-OCT2026

Open https://app.crustdata.com and select “Have a promo code?” below Continue. Add the code before signing up with your email. Use email signup, not “Continue with Google”, so the code can be applied. Already have an account, or need help? Contact the neatHack organisers at https://neatlogs.com/discord.

API documentation: https://www.crustdata.com/api-documentation

Before you build
Every project must use neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai. Keep evidence of all three for your submission and demo.

Hackathon guide: https://neatlogs.com/hackathon

Build-log skill: https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/skill

View your team: https://neatlogs.com/hackathon/check-in

Get help on Discord: https://neatlogs.com/discord

See you at neatHack!

The neatlogs team i wANNA DO THIS

Planning

* **Watch a running system**An agent watches a running system for unusual behavior. When the agent finds a problem, it looks for the cause and takes an action to fix it.
* **Several agents working together**Several worker agents each solve part of a task on their own. A coordinator agent then combines their results and settles any disagreements.
* **Work while things change**An agent works on a long task while the environment it works in keeps changing.

Entire is the git forge for AI-native teams. The Entire CLI captures every AI coding agent session, so the reasoning behind the code stays with the git repo, right next to your code. Then, Continuous Memory (Entire Graph + Entire Brain) turns those sessions into living knowledge for your agents. Your repo learns from every attempt, every fix, every decision, and your agents get smarter because of it.

Connect a Git commit to the agent sessions and decisions behind it.

You or your agent can search semantically through previous commits, sessions, and decisions, or literal source text, across pushed, indexed repositories.

Go to app.neatlogs.com. Use **Continue with Google**, or type your email. The page asks for a work email, then finds your team or helps you create a workspace.

The sign-up screen. Signing up only works in a browser, so a coding agent can't do this step for you.

Then create an organization and a project if it asks. Your traces live inside the project.

2

## Copy your project API key

1 min

Open **Settings, then API keys**. You will see two keys. They are not the same thing.

Top: Project API key. Bottom: HTTP ingest key (starts with nlw\_).

**Use this one**The **Project API key** (the top one). Click **Reveal key** then **Copy key**. The SDK wants this.

**Not this one**The **HTTP ingest key** that starts with `nlw_` is for raw HTTP calls. If you give it to the SDK you get a 401.

Put the key in an environment variable. Don't paste it into code, chat, or git.

```
export NEATLOGS_API_KEY="paste-your-project-key-here"
```

3

## Add the SDK to your app

3 min

```
pip install neatlogs openai
```

```
import os, neatlogs
from openai import OpenAI

neatlogs.init(api_key=os.environ["NEATLOGS_API_KEY"], workflow_name="my-first-app")
client = neatlogs.wrap(OpenAI())

r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "capital of Spain?"}],
)
print(r.choices[0].message.content)

neatlogs.flush()      # send anything still waiting
neatlogs.shutdown()
```

That is the whole change: `init` once, `wrap` your client, and `flush` before the script ends.

```
npm install neatlogs openai
```

```
import { init, shutdown, wrapOpenAI } from 'neatlogs';
import OpenAI from 'openai';

await init({ apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY, workflowName: 'my-first-app' });
const client = wrapOpenAI(new OpenAI());

const r = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'gpt-4o',
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'capital of Spain?' }],
});
console.log(r.choices[0].message.content);

await shutdown();   // sends anything still waiting
```

**Other frameworks**Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini, Vertex, OpenRouter, Agno, CrewAI and pydantic-ai are covered in the docs index. LangChain needs one extra line: pass `neatlogs.langchain_handler()` in your callbacks. Without it nothing is traced.

4

## Check that it works

1 min

Run the built-in check before your own app. It sends a test trace and reads it back using only your project key.

```
python -m neatlogs doctor --probe
```

You want to see `TRACE_VISIBLE` and `TRACE_FINALIZED` marked PASS. Then run your app:

```
python app.py
```

5

## See your trace

1 min

Open **Traces**. A new row appears within a few seconds, with your input and the model's answer.

The Traces tab. The "capital of Spain?" row is the one we just made.

Click the row to open it. You see the workflow, each model call, tokens, and the output.

One trace: the question, the model call (gpt-4o), and the answer.

**That's it.**Everything below is optional: letting a coding agent do the setup, and reading traces back from the terminal.

A

Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar. Do steps 1 and 2 yourself first, because sign-up happens in a browser. Then paste this note and the prompt below into your agent.

I already signed up at app.neatlogs.com and made a project.
My project API key is in the NEATLOGS_API_KEY environment variable (not the nlw_ HTTP key).

**Option A — Extend `job-apply-agent`: "Application Autopilot"** (recommended if you want low build risk)
Resume + job URLs in → agent researches each company via Crustdata, matches fit, drafts tailored cover letter, submits to a scoped set of portals, tracks state across runs, retries failures, verifies confirmation. **Option B — "Source-Conflicting Research Agent"** (recommended for max score confidence)

Matches the hackathon's flagship example, bounded and verifiable (citations are checkable), clean demo, low flake risk. Less original, but delivery is near-certain.

**Option C — "Self-Watching Pipeline"** (most impressive, highest risk)
Your agent monitors its *own* neatlogs traces, detects failures/anomalies, diagnoses root cause, adjusts strategy, re-runs. The neatlogs evidence story is unbeatable — but solo scope in 48h is tight. Effectively A + a supervisor layer; only pick if A feels done by Sunday morning.

All three use Crustdata, all three give you a natural "baseline trace → failure → fix → improved trace" loop for the 30%+25%.

# neatHack Plan: **Ouroboros** — the self-watching agent pipeline

## Concept

A **worker agent** completes a substantial task — generating verified company dossiers from a domain (Crustdata company/people data + web cross-check + structured output) — with every run fully traced in neatlogs. A **supervisor agent** then reads its *own* traces through the neatlogs CLI, diagnoses what failed, applies a remediation (backoff, alternate tool, plan revision), re-runs, and verifies the fix.

The judges' hard-to-fake evidence — *"the agent recovers from failures: a run where an action failed, showing what it did next"* — becomes the product itself. And neatlogs' per-trace cost/token data feeds directly into the cfo.ai business plan.

## Why it scores

| Criterion | Weight | How we hit it |
|---|---|---|
| The agent | 30% | Recovery, verification, iteration, state across runs — all are the judge focus list |
| Tool usage | 25% | neatlogs **readback** (traces as an input to reasoning, not just output), Entire checkpoints on every fix, cfo.ai unit economics from trace costs |
| Demo | 20% | Visual story: red failing trace → supervisor diagnosis → green fixed trace |
| Public building | 15% | 3+ #neatHack posts including the interesting failure moment |
| Originality | 10% | An agent that watches and heals itself |

## Architecture (Python, boring and observable)

```
ouroboros/
├── worker/          # dossier agent: plan → Crustdata tools → web cross-check → verify → dossier.json
├── supervisor/      # reads neatlogs traces → classifies failure → remediation → rerun → verify
├── state/           # JSONL run log (state across runs, retries, dedup)
├── scripts/         # demo_run.sh — the exact command sequence in the video
└── hackathon.md     # official build log
```

Runs: `python -m ouro run --domain x.com` and `python -m ouro supervise --window 1h`

## Timeline (IST)

**Today, Sat Oct 10**
- **2:00–3:30 PM** — Setup: Crustdata (code `NEATLOGS-OCT2026`, email signup), neatlogs (Project API key, `doctor --probe` must PASS), Entire (`brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire`, repo + first checkpoint), cfo.ai (signup + immediate cancel). New public repo with initial commit — hackathon clock starts.
- **3:30–7:00 PM** — Worker v1: Crustdata tools + dossier pipeline, neatlogs wrapped from commit #1.
- **7:00–10:00 PM** — Batch run across several domains; capture first real failing run as **Trace T1** (baseline).
- Wrap: commit + checkpoint, `hackathon.md`, post #1 with the T1 failure trace.

**Sunday Oct 11**
- **Morning** — Supervisor v1: `neatlogs traces list/get --json` readback, failure classifier, remediation chooser.
- **Afternoon** — Remediation + rerun → **Trace T2** (the money pair). Verification self-check passes.
- **Evening** — Improvement loop #2 (prompt/plan revision → T3/T4 pair), Entire graph + checkpoints, posts #2/#3, Discord presence.
- **Night** — cfo.ai business plan: pull per-dossier cost from neatlogs trace data, model pricing/revenue/runway.

**Monday Oct 12**
- **Morning** — Record 3-min demo: problem → red trace → supervisor → green trace → checkpoints → cfo.ai numbers.
- **Afternoon** — README, repo polish, submission rehearsal. **Hard stop: submission-ready by noon.**
- **7:00 PM** — Submit early (quote-tweet: team *um*, name, public repo, demo + form). Buffer to 11:55 PM.

## Risks & mitigations

- **Entire agent support** — check `entire enable --agent <name>` for opencode; if absent, route commits through Codex/Claude Code for capture. *Verify in Phase 0.*
- **neatlogs CLI login** — device login needs your browser approval; do it during setup, not at 2 AM Monday.
- **Crustdata rate limits** — the expected failure mode, which is the point; supervisor handles with cache+backoff.
- **cfo.ai credits timing** — team-granted; ping Discord if not visible by Mon morning.
- **Sleep** — the Mon-noon hard stop exists so tired Monday-you still submits.

## Submission evidence checklist

- [ ] Before/after trace pairs with compared numbers (T1 vs T2, plus one more pair)
- [ ] Entire checkpoint link: `entire.io/gh/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<SHA>`
- [ ] cfo.ai business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway) in submission
- [ ] Public repo, commits all dated Oct 10–12
- [ ] Demo video + #neatHack posts
- [ ] `hackathon.md` build log at repo root

A company search API is a programmatic interface for finding businesses by specific criteria. Common filters include industry, geography, employee count, funding stage, and tech stack. You send a request and receive structured JSON. This data can feed your product, data pipeline, or internal tool.

Developers use company search APIs for four main purposes. First, building targeted prospect lists for sales workflows. Second, enriching CRM records with missing firmographics. Third, running repeatable market scans. Fourth, giving AI agents accurate company context at decision time.

The tricky part is that “company data” isn’t one thing: different providers trade off speed, freshness, coverage, and cost in ways that affect how you architect your integration.

Join us as we go through the basics – how search differs from enrichment, how filters and pagination work, and how to handle limits and errors in production – using Crustdata’s APIs for concrete examples.

## Understanding company data APIs

“Company data API” is an umbrella term. Some APIs are built to help you discover companies that match a set of filters. Others are built to enrich a company you already know about.

Before you implement anything, it’s worth separating those patterns and understanding where the underlying data comes from, because that determines what you can trust, what you have to verify, and how you should design your workflow.

### What is a company search API?

A company search API is a query interface that returns companies matching the criteria you provide. Most implementations use REST architecture. These APIs answer discovery questions like "Which companies match these characteristics?" They differ from lookup APIs that retrieve details about a known company.

In a real system, search is typically the first stage. You use it to produce a set of candidate companies, then pass those results into the next step in your pipeline.

For example:

* Prospecting workflows use search to build target account lists, then sync them into a CRM or outreach tool.
* Market and competitive research uses search to create cohorts for analysis, like “all fintechs headquartered in New York above 50 employees.
* AI agents and automation use search to pull the current context right before taking an action, like drafting a message or triggering an alert.

Where do these APIs get company information? Well, most providers aggregate from multiple sources and normalize everything into a consistent schema, which is why the same company can have different categories or event history across vendors.

Data sources are wide-ranging:

* Government registries provide legal entity names, incorporation dates, registered addresses, and status where available.
* Professional data and job postings inform employee counts, job titles, and hiring signals derived from public profiles and recruiting pages.
* Funding and corporate activity databases track rounds, investors, acquisitions, and related timelines, often with strong coverage of startups.
* Web crawling and news sources capture website changes, press releases, careers pages, and recent mentions that signal momentum.
* Review and marketplace platforms can add product categories and some stack clues via sites like G2 or Glassdoor.

Different providers focus on specific areas and use different sources. OpenCorporates is oriented around legal entity and registry data, which fits verification and compliance use cases. Crunchbase is oriented around startups, investors, funding rounds, and M&A. Crustdata’s positioning is more about fresh signals and monitoring across venture capital, sales, and recruitment, which makes a difference when you care about what changed recently, not just what’s in a periodic snapshot.

Some company APIs include technology fields. Meaningful technographics often come from dedicated services. This data is typically inferred rather than declared by the company. Common methods include scanning websites for scripts and tags, checking HTTP headers, and extracting mentions of tools from job postings.

If your workflow depends heavily on “uses Salesforce” or “runs on AWS,” you may end up combining a company search API with a technographics provider.

A useful comparison point across vendors is update behavior. Some refresh on a schedule, which works for periodic list building and batch enrichment. Others support on-demand refresh or continuous monitoring, which is a better fit for event-triggered workflows.

### Search vs enrichment: two different patterns

Search and enrichment solve different problems, and they’re often priced and rate-limited differently.

A search API takes criteria and returns a list of matching companies. Use it when discovering accounts by filters. This pattern works when you don't know the company set in advance.

An enrichment API takes an identifier like a domain or company ID and returns a detailed profile for that one company. Use it when you already have the account, and you’re filling in missing fields or verifying details.

In Crustdata, the company search endpoints handle discovery, while the company enrichment endpoint (

```
/screener/company
```

) handles lookups by domain or ID.

Cost usually follows the pattern too: search is commonly priced based on how many results you pull, and enrichment is commonly priced per company enriched, with real-time refresh typically costing more than cached enrichment.

## Working with filters and search criteria

Once you understand what a company search API returns, the next step is learning how to ask the right questions.

Most of the power lives in the filter layer. Filters decide what the API can express, how much work you push onto the provider versus your own code, and how stable your results are when the vendor’s taxonomy changes.

### Anatomy of a search request

A search request is a structured API call with three components: authentication, filter payload, and pagination controls. Crustdata's company search uses a POST request with a JSON body. Query parameters are not used.

Authentication is handled by passing your API token in the request header using

```
Authorization: Bearer <your_token>
```

. This is typical for company data APIs and lets you rotate keys without changing application code.

The body of the request contains a list of filters. Each filter is an object with three required parts:

* ```
  filter_type
  ```

  identifies the field you want to filter on, such as industry, region, or company headcount.
* ```
  type
  ```

  defines the operator, like inclusion, exclusion, or a range comparison.
* ```
  value
  ```

  supplies the criteria the operator evaluates against.

When you combine filters in a single request, they are evaluated together.

For example, finding technology companies in the United States with 51 to 200 employees means sending three filters in the same request: one for industry, one for region, and one for headcount. A company must satisfy all of them to appear in the results.

A useful mental model is that search generates a candidate set. Anything you can’t express cleanly in filters will either require additional queries or a post-processing step on your side.

### Using an autocomplete API to find valid filter values

Filters fail in boring ways. The most common one is “your value doesn’t match what the provider expects.” Industry labels and other categorical fields often need to match a canonical vocabulary, including capitalization.

Many providers offer an autocomplete-like API or published value lists to help you discover the exact values you should use. This is especially useful when you’re building a UI where users type free text, and you need to map that input onto the provider’s taxonomy.

Autocomplete is available for multiple categories, including:

* Region, to return valid geography values you can paste directly into filters.
* Industry, to return canonical industry labels rather than whatever a user typed.
* Title, to help when you’re building people-adjacent workflows that depend on role data.
* School, to support education-related fields in products that blend company and talent signals.

A practical workflow involves resolving user input against the provider’s suggested values during setup or at query time, storing the returned value, and then using that exact string in your filter.

### Filter types and operators

Different fields expect different operator types, and using the wrong operator for a field type causes errors.

Text-like filters typically support inclusion and exclusion. You pass a list of accepted values for in, or a list of blocked values for

```
not in
```

. This is common for categories like industry and region.

Numeric filters use ranges. Crustdata supports

```
between
```

with minimum and maximum values, and some fields also support a unit or currency qualifier through an extra sub-field. Revenue is the typical example.

Some filters behave like flags. In Crustdata,

```
IN_THE_NEWS
```

is one of these: you’re not comparing against a value, you’re turning a condition on.

By default, multiple filters combine with

```
AND
```

logic, meaning every condition must be true. If you need

```
OR
```

logic, the usual approach is to run separate searches and union the results on your side.

### Common search scenarios

Most real-world queries are variations on a few repeatable patterns:

* ICP list building combines industry, region, and headcount to generate a starting account set you can enrich or score.
* Budget-aware narrowing adds revenue ranges or employee buckets to reduce the result size before exporting to downstream tools.
* Activity-driven discovery uses hiring-related filters like job opportunities to find companies that are actively staffing roles.
* Exclusions for focus apply

  ```
  not in
  ```

  to filter out regions or industries you explicitly don’t want in your output.

The key is to treat search as iterative. Run a first pass, inspect what comes back, then refine filters until the query produces a stable, useful result set for your workflow.

## Implementation guide

With the concepts and filters in place, you can wire everything together in a way that’s predictable and cost-aware.

Let’s go over a complete implementation flow.

### Choosing the right endpoint: realtime vs in-database search

Crustdata exposes two company search endpoints that solve different problems:

* Realtime search is optimized for fresh data. It checks the internet in real time. Pricing is typically based on the number of companies returned. Pagination uses fixed-size pages with a maximum page cap per query.
* In-database search queries a pre-indexed database. It’s optimized for bulk discovery and rich, nested filtering. It’s generally more cost-efficient for large result sets and supports larger page sizes. Pagination is often cursor-based rather than page-based, which makes it easier to stream through large result sets and pinpoint specific companies.

Use realtime search when the question depends on what’s true right now, like whether a company is actively hiring or just announced funding.

Use an in-database search when you’re building large lists, running scheduled jobs, or doing exploratory analysis where being slightly out of date is acceptable.

There’s also a structural difference in how filters are expressed. Realtime search uses an array of filter objects with

```
filter_type
```

,

```
type
```

, and

```
value
```

. In-database search uses a nested filters object with an explicit logical operator and a list of conditions.

If you switch endpoints, you can’t reuse the same payload verbatim.

### Setting up your environment

Before writing any code, you’ll need to set up credentials and basic request handling.

Store your Crustdata API token in an environment variable, such as

```
CRUSTDATA_API_TOKEN
```

, and read it at runtime. Hardcoding tokens makes rotation painful and increases the risk of accidental leaks.

Crustdata’s API is JSON over HTTP and doesn’t require an SDK. You can use any language with an HTTP client. Python is a common choice for data pipelines and automation jobs, so the example below uses plain

```
requests
```

without any wrappers.

### A minimal Python example

Here’s a Python script that uses Crustdata to programmatically discover and list specific business leads.

It authenticates via an API token to filter for U.S.-based software companies with a headcount between 51 and 200 employees. Once the request is processed, it iterates through the results to extract and print the names of every matching organization.

```

### Handling pagination and parsing results

Search results almost never fit in a single response, so pagination handling needs to be part of your implementation.

Realtime search returns a fixed number of companies per page. You increment the page parameter starting at 1 and stop when the companies array comes back empty, or you hit the maximum page limit. Because pages are capped, you should treat realtime search as a targeted query tool rather than a bulk export mechanism.

In-database search uses cursor-based pagination. You omit the cursor on the first request, then pass the cursor value from the response into the next request. This continues until no cursor is returned. You can also control batch size with a

```
limit
```

parameter, up to the documented maximum.

Both endpoints return a list of companies plus a count field that tells you how many matches exist. Use that count early. If a query produces far more results than you expect, it’s usually cheaper to tighten filters than to page through everything.

When you hit pagination limits, the usual workaround is to split the query into smaller chunks. For example, run the same search once per industry category or per region, then merge the results on your side.

## Limitations and best practices

Company search APIs work best when you design around their limits instead of discovering them in production. Factors like rate limits and pagination caps shape how aggressive your queries can be and where you should add guardrails.

### Rate limits, pagination caps, and credit usage

Each endpoint enforces limits to protect the service and keep costs within bounds.

For realtime search, Crustdata applies rate limits to protect the service. Requests beyond the allowed threshold return rate-limit errors.

If you need higher throughput, it’s usually possible to discuss custom rate limits with the provider, which is common when teams move from prototyping to production workloads.

Pagination behavior differs by endpoint and affects how much data you can realistically pull in one pass.

Realtime search paginates by page number and features a maximum page limit. This design makes it a targeted query tool for high-intent leads rather than a bulk export mechanism.

In-database search uses cursor-based pagination and supports much larger result sets, but you still get better performance and lower cost when filters are specific rather than broad.

Credits are typically consumed based on results returned, not just requests sent. Realtime-style search tends to be priced per company returned, while database-style search is usually more cost-efficient for large batches.

It’s common for test queries that return zero companies to have little or no cost impact, which makes it safe to iterate on filters during development.

These mechanics mean it’s smarter to use realtime search sparingly for questions where freshness matters, and in-database search for bulk discovery and scheduled jobs.

### Error handling and optimization

Most errors fall into a small set of predictable cases.

A 400-level error usually means the filter payload is malformed. This often comes from using invalid values for categorical fields. Validating inputs with an autocomplete API before sending a search request avoids most of these failures.

A 429 response means you’ve hit a rate limit. The safest response is to slow down, not retry immediately. Space requests evenly across the minute and apply exponential backoff so short bursts don’t cascade into repeated failures.

Cost control comes from tightening queries early. Narrow filters reduce result size, which reduces both pagination overhead and credit usage. For large list building or exploratory analysis, in-database search is almost always cheaper than realtime search.

Data freshness also benefits from selective refresh. Firmographic fields like industry or headquarters change infrequently and can be cached locally. Time-sensitive signals like job postings or recent activity are better fetched on demand.

For very high-volume use cases, some providers also offer bulk datasets delivered via cloud storage. A common pattern is to use bulk data as a baseline, then layer API calls on top only for real-time checks or monitoring.

## Start building with company data

Once you understand the basics of company search APIs, you’re in a position to build something that holds up in production.

The difference between a quick proof of concept and a reliable integration usually comes down to making deliberate choices early, like validating inputs before requests go out and selecting the search mode that matches how fresh the data needs to be.

Company data becomes most valuable when it’s wired directly into real workflows, whether that’s an AI sales agent making decisions in real time or a prospecting tool that refreshes as the market changes.

If you’re ready to move from exploration to implementation, book a demo with Crustdata to walk through your use case and get API access.

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import subprocess
import sys
import uuid

from .config import settings
from .state import read_runs
from .trace import init_tracing, shutdown_tracing
from .worker import run_dossier


def _doctor() -> int:
    print(f"model:                {settings.model}")
    print(f"OPENAI_API_KEY:       {'set' if settings.openai_api_key else 'MISSING'}")
    print(f"NEATLOGS_API_KEY:     {'set' if settings.neatlogs_api_key else 'MISSING'}")
    print(f"CRUSTDATA_API_KEY:    {'set' if settings.crustdata_api_key else 'MISSING'}")
    print(f"OURO_FAULT_INJECT:    {settings.fault_inject}")

    if settings.neatlogs_api_key:
        proc = subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, "-m", "neatlogs", "doctor", "--probe"],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=120,
        )
        print("\n--- neatlogs doctor --probe ---")
        print(proc.stdout.strip() or proc.stderr.strip())

    if settings.crustdata_api_key:
        from .tools.crustdata import CrustdataClient, CrustdataError

        client = CrustdataClient()
        try:
            endpoints = client.account_endpoints()
            print("\n--- crustdata /account/endpoints ---")
            print(json.dumps(endpoints, indent=2, default=str)[:1500])
        except CrustdataError as exc:
            print(f"\ncrustdata check failed: {exc} (status={exc.status})")

    missing = [n for n, v in [("OPENAI_API_KEY", settings.openai_api_key), ("NEATLOGS_API_KEY", settings.neatlogs_api_key), ("CRUSTDATA_API_KEY", settings.crustdata_api_key)] if not v]
    if missing:
        print(f"\nmissing keys: {', '.join(missing)}")
        return 1
    return 0


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="ouro")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    run_p = sub.add_parser("run", help="Run the dossier worker for one domain")
    run_p.add_argument("domain")

    batch_p = sub.add_parser("batch", help="Run the dossier worker for a comma-separated domain list")
    batch_p.add_argument("domains")

    sup_p = sub.add_parser("supervise", help="Watch recent runs and heal failures")
    sup_p.add_argument("--window-hours", type=float, default=24)
    sup_p.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true")

    sub.add_parser("doctor", help="Check keys, neatlogs probe, and Crustdata endpoint access")
    sub.add_parser("runs", help="Show the run log")

    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    if args.command == "doctor":
        return _doctor()
    if args.command == "runs":
        for row in read_runs():
            print(json.dumps({k: row.get(k) for k in ("run_id", "domain", "status", "duration_s")}, default=str))
        return 0

    run_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
    tracker = init_tracing(run_id)
    try:
        if args.command == "run":
            record = run_dossier(args.domain)
            print(json.dumps({k: record.get(k) for k in ("run_id", "domain", "status", "duration_s", "schema_issues", "verify_issues")}, indent=2))
            return 0 if record["status"] == "success" else 2
        if args.command == "batch":
            domains = [d.strip() for d in args.domains.split(",") if d.strip()]
            records = [run_dossier(d) for d in domains]
            print(json.dumps([{ "domain": r["domain"], "status": r["status"], "run_id": r["run_id"]} for r in records], indent=2))
            return 0 if all(r["status"] == "success" for r in records) else 2
        if args.command == "supervise":
            from .supervisor import supervise

            reports = supervise(args.window_hours, rerun=not args.dry_run)
            print(json.dumps(reports, indent=2, default=str)[:4000])
            return 0
    finally:
        shutdown_tracing(tracker)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

    runs = read_runs()

def test_validate_dossier_flags_missing_sections():
    issues = validate_dossier({"domain": "x.com", "overview": "hi"}, {"tools_succeeded": ["identify_company"], "company_id": "c1"})

    assert not any("company never resolved" in i for i in issues)


def test_validate_dossier_flags_no_evidence():
    issues = validate_dossier({}, {})
    assert issues


def test_parse_json_object_handles_fences():
    assert parse_json_object('```json\n{"a": 1}\n```') == {"a": 1}
    assert parse_json_object("noise {\"b\": 2} tail") == {"b": 2}
    assert parse_json_object("plain text") == {}


def test_crustdata_fault_injection_first_call_fails():
    def handler(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
        return httpx.Response(200, json={"companies": [{"company_id": "c-1"}]})

    http = httpx.Client(transport=httpx.MockTransport(handler), base_url="https://api.crustdata.com")
    client = CrustdataClient(token="fake", http=http)
    client.fault_inject = True
    with pytest.raises(CrustdataError) as exc:
        client.identify("x.com")
    assert exc.value.status == 429
    result = client.identify("x.com")
    assert result["companies"][0]["company_id"] == "c-1"


def test_crustdata_records_http_error():
    def handler(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
        return httpx.Response(403, json={"error": "forbidden"})

    http = httpx.Client(transport=httpx.MockTransport(handler), base_url="https://api.crustdata.com")
    client = CrustdataClient(token="fake", http=http)
    with pytest.raises(CrustdataError) as exc:
        client.web_search("q")
    assert exc.value.status == 403
    assert client.calls[-1]["status"] == 403

# Ouroboros

An agent pipeline that watches itself die, then fixes itself.

**neatHack 2026 project (team *um*, solo build).** Built for the "Build an agent that works (literally)" track.

## The idea

Most agent demos show the happy path. Ouroboros treats failure as the feature:

1. **Worker** (`ouro/worker/dossier.py`) — given a company domain, it plans, calls Crustdata tools (identify → enrich → people → web search), and synthesizes a verified company dossier. Every LLM call, tool call, and failure is traced in **neatlogs**.
2. **Supervisor** (`ouro/supervisor/heal.py`) — reads the worker's run log and its *own* neatlogs traces, classifies each failure (429s, missing data, verification gaps), picks a remediation, re-runs, and verifies the fix.

The judges' hard-to-fake evidence — *a run where an action failed, showing what the agent did next* — is the product itself.

## Layout

```
ouro/
├── worker/dossier.py     # dossier agent: plan -> tools -> synthesize -> verify
├── supervisor/heal.py    # trace/run-log reader, failure classifier, remediation
├── tools/crustdata.py    # Crustdata API client (with optional fault injection)
├── state.py              # JSONL run log (state across runs)
└── trace.py              # neatlogs init/shutdown
```

## Setup

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"
cp .env.example .env   # fill in keys
```

Env vars:

| Var | Where from |
|---|---|
| `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY` | Crustdata dashboard (hackathon promo code `NEATLOGS-OCT2026`) |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | OpenAI |
| `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` | app.neatlogs.com → Settings → API keys → **top** key (Project API key, not the `nlw_` ingest key) |

Optional: `OURO_MODEL` (default `gpt-4o`), `OURO_FAULT_INJECT=1` (deterministic first-call 429 per endpoint, for repeatable demo runs).

## Usage

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m ouro doctor                 # keys + neatlogs probe + crustdata endpoint access
.venv/bin/python -m ouro run crustdata.com      # one dossier (traced)
.venv/bin/python -m ouro batch a.com,b.com      # batch, state across runs
.venv/bin/python -m ouro runs                   # run log summary
.venv/bin/python -m ouro supervise --window-hours 24   # classify failures, remediate, rerun
```

Outputs land in `out/<domain>/<run_id>/` (`dossier.json`, `run.json`); the run log is `state/runs.jsonl`.

## Tests

```bash
.venv/bin/pytest -q   # offline: state log, fault injection, schema validation
```

def run_dossier(
    domain: str,
    out_root: Path | None = None,
    llm: Any | None = None,
    client: CrustdataClient | None = None,
    remediation: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    run_id = uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]
    started = time.monotonic()
    out_root = out_root or Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent.parent / "out"
    if client is None:
        if settings.mock_mode:
            from ..fakes import MockCrustdata

            client = MockCrustdata()
        else:
            client = CrustdataClient()
    if llm is None:
        llm = _llm()
    actions = list((remediation or {}).get("actions", []))
    issues = list((remediation or {}).get("issues", []))
    backoff = "retry_with_backoff" in actions
    system = _SYSTEM
    if issues:
        system += (
            "\nRemediation: the previous attempt had these issues and you must fix them: "
            + "; ".join(issues)
            + ". Do not leave any dossier section empty."
        )
    if "revise_plan_expand_search" in actions:
        system += "\nRemediation: run web_search for recent news before finalizing."
    evidence: dict[str, Any] = {
        "domain": domain,
        "tool_results": {},
        "tools_succeeded": [],
        "tool_failures": [],
        "company_id": None,
    }

    messages: list[dict[str, Any]] = [
        {"role": "system", "content": system},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Build a dossier for: {domain}"},
    ]

    dossier: dict[str, Any] = {}
    steps = 0
    usage = {"prompt_tokens": 0, "completion_tokens": 0}
    for _ in range(12):
        steps += 1
        resp = llm.chat.completions.create(model=settings.model, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
        _accumulate_usage(resp, usage)
        msg = resp.choices[0].message
        messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True))
        if not msg.tool_calls:
            dossier = parse_json_object(msg.content or "")
            break
        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            args = json.loads(call.function.arguments or "{}")
            try:
                result = _call_tool(call.function.name, args, client, backoff=backoff)
                evidence["tools_succeeded"].append(call.function.name)
                evidence["tool_results"][call.function.name] = result
                if call.function.name == "identify_company" and isinstance(result, dict):
                    evidence["company_id"] = _extract_company_id(result)
                payload = json.dumps(result, default=str)[:6000]
            except CrustdataError as exc:
                evidence["tool_failures"].append(
                    {"tool": call.function.name, "args": args, "status": exc.status, "error": str(exc)}
                )
                payload = json.dumps({"error": str(exc), "status": exc.status})
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": payload})

    schema_issues = validate_dossier(dossier, evidence)
    verdict = _verify(domain, dossier, evidence, llm=llm)
    passed = verdict.get("passed", False) and not schema_issues

    run_record: dict[str, Any] = {
        "run_id": run_id,
        "domain": domain,
        "status": "success" if passed else "failed",
        "started_epoch": time.time(),
        "duration_s": round(time.monotonic() - started, 2),
        "steps": steps,
        "tools_succeeded": sorted(set(evidence["tools_succeeded"])),
        "tool_failures": evidence["tool_failures"],
        "schema_issues": schema_issues,
        "verify_issues": verdict.get("issues", []),
        "llm_calls": len([m for m in messages if m.get("role") == "assistant"]),
        "tool_calls": client.calls,
        "usage": usage,
        "remediation": actions,
    }

    out_dir = out_root / domain.replace(".", "_") / run_id
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (out_dir / "dossier.json").write_text(json.dumps(dossier, indent=2, default=str))
    (out_dir / "run.json").write_text(json.dumps(run_record, indent=2, default=str))
    append_run(run_record)
    return run_record


def _accumulate_usage(resp: Any, usage: dict[str, int]) -> None:
    resp_usage = getattr(resp, "usage", None)
    if resp_usage is None:
        return
    for key in ("prompt_tokens", "completion_tokens"):
        value = getattr(resp_usage, key, None)
        if isinstance(value, int):
            usage[key] += value

    append_run(run_record)

def test_mock_worker_fails_when_tools_fail(tmp_path, monkeypatch):

    assert len(reports) == 1

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Aggregate dossier run records into the cost/throughput numbers for the cfo.ai business plan."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
OUT_DIR = ROOT / "out"


def summarize(runs: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    successes = [r for r in runs if r.get("status") == "success"]
    failures = [r for r in runs if r.get("status") != "success"]
    durations = [float(r.get("duration_s") or 0) for r in runs]
    failures_by_status: dict[str, int] = {}
    for run in failures:
        for failure in run.get("tool_failures", []):
            key = str(failure.get("status") or "unknown")
            failures_by_status[key] = failures_by_status.get(key, 0) + 1
    healed = [r for r in successes if r.get("remediation")]
    return {
        "runs": len(runs),
        "successes": len(successes),
        "failures": len(failures),
        "success_rate": round(len(successes) / len(runs), 3) if runs else None,
        "healed_by_supervisor": len(healed),
        "avg_duration_s": round(sum(durations) / len(durations), 2) if durations else None,
        "tool_calls_total": sum(len(r.get("tool_calls", [])) for r in runs),
        "llm_calls_total": sum(int(r.get("llm_calls", 0)) for r in runs),
        "prompt_tokens_total": sum(int((r.get("usage") or {}).get("prompt_tokens", 0)) for r in runs),
        "completion_tokens_total": sum(int((r.get("usage") or {}).get("completion_tokens", 0)) for r in runs),
        "failures_by_http_status": failures_by_status,
    }


def load_runs(out_dir: Path) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    runs: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for path in sorted(out_dir.glob("*/*/run.json")):
        try:
            runs.append(json.loads(path.read_text()))
        except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError):
            continue
    return runs


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--out-dir", type=Path, default=OUT_DIR)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(json.dumps(summarize(load_runs(args.out_dir)), indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

## Usage

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m ouro doctor                      # keys + neatlogs probe + crustdata endpoint access
.venv/bin/python -m ouro run crustdata.com           # one dossier (traced)

```

Outputs land in `out/<domain>/<run_id>/` (`dossier.json`, `run.json`); the run log is `state/runs.jsonl`.

```bash
bash scripts/demo.sh

`scripts/trace_costs.py` aggregates `out/**/run.json` into success rate, failure counts, token usage, and durations — the inputs for the cfo.ai unit-economics model.

## Product

Company dossiers produced by an agent that verifies its own work and heals its own failures. Runners: sales teams, recruitors, investors doing account research today.

| Line | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| LLM tokens (prompt) | TO FILL | trace_costs.py `prompt_tokens_total / runs` |

## Pricing

| Plan | Price | Includes |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 1 dossier, no supervisor |
| Pro | $29/mo | 50 dossiers, auto-heal, exports |
| Team | $99/mo | 300 dossiers, batch mode, shared state |

## Revenue scenarios (cfo.ai)

| Scenario | Customers | Dossiers/mo | Revenue | Infra+inference | Gross margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- Build cost so far: TO FILL (credits used during hackathon)
- Position at submission: pre-seed / self-funded, hackathon credits carry first 3 months
- Break-even customer count: TO FILL (fixed infra ÷ contribution margin per customer)

    report = plan_remediation(run)
    report["traces_seen"] = len(read_recent_traces())
    issues = list(run.get("schema_issues", [])) + list(run.get("verify_issues", []))
    remediation = {"actions": report["actions"], "issues": issues}
    after = run_dossier(run["domain"], out_root=out_root, llm=llm, client=client, remediation=remediation)
    report["remediation_applied"] = remediation
    report["before"] = {
        "status": run.get("status"),
        "schema_issues": run.get("schema_issues", []),
        "verify_issues": run.get("verify_issues", []),
        "duration_s": run.get("duration_s"),
    }
    report["after"] = {
        "status": after.get("status"),
        "schema_issues": after.get("schema_issues", []),
        "verify_issues": after.get("verify_issues", []),
        "duration_s": after.get("duration_s"),
    }
    report["healed"] = run.get("status") != "success" and after.get("status") == "success"
    return report

    rerun: bool = True,
    llm: Any | None = None,
    client: Any | None = None,
    out_root: Any | None = None,
) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    reports: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for run in failed_runs(window_hours):

        if rerun:

from __future__ import annotations

import json

from ouro import state
from ouro.fakes import MockCrustdata, MockLLM, build_worker_script
from ouro.supervisor.heal import load_watch_state, watch_daemon, watch_once
from ouro.worker import run_dossier


def _patch_state(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(state, "LOG_PATH", tmp_path / "runs.jsonl")


def _failing_mock():
    client = MockCrustdata()
    client.fault_inject = True
    return client


def _healing_mock():
    client = MockCrustdata()
    client.fault_inject = True
    return client


def test_watch_once_heals_new_failure_and_records_it(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    _patch_state(tmp_path, monkeypatch)
    run_dossier(
        "example.com",
        out_root=tmp_path / "out",
        llm=MockLLM(build_worker_script()),
        client=_failing_mock(),
    )
    result = watch_once(24, llm=MockLLM(build_worker_script()), client=_healing_mock(), out_root=tmp_path / "out")
    assert result["healed"] != []
    ws = load_watch_state()
    assert len(ws["healed_run_ids"]) == len(result["healed"])
    assert ws["cycles"] == 1
    assert ws["started_at"] is not None


def test_watch_once_does_not_reheal(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    _patch_state(tmp_path, monkeypatch)
    run_dossier(
        "example.com",
        out_root=tmp_path / "out",
        llm=MockLLM(build_worker_script()),
        client=_failing_mock(),
    )
    first = watch_once(24, llm=MockLLM(build_worker_script()), client=_healing_mock(), out_root=tmp_path / "out")
    assert len(first["healed"]) == 1
    second = watch_once(24, llm=MockLLM(build_worker_script()), client=_healing_mock(), out_root=tmp_path / "out")
    assert second["seen"] == []
    assert second["healed"] == []
    ws = load_watch_state()
    assert ws["cycles"] == 2
    assert len(ws["healed_run_ids"]) == 1


def test_watch_daemon_terminates_on_max_cycles(tmp_path, monkeypatch, capsys):
    _patch_state(tmp_path, monkeypatch)
    cycles = watch_daemon(
        window_hours=24,
        interval_s=0,
        max_cycles=2,
        llm=MockLLM(build_worker_script()),
        client=_healing_mock(),
        out_root=tmp_path / "out",
    )
    assert cycles == 2
    out = capsys.readouterr().out
    lines = [line for line in out.splitlines() if line.startswith("{")]
    assert len(lines) == 2
    assert all("cycle" in json.loads(line) for line in lines)

1: # Ouroboros
2: 
3: An agent pipeline that watches itself die, then fixes itself.
4: 
5: **neatHack 2026 project (team *um*, solo build).** Built for the "Build an agent that works (literally)" track.
6: 
7: ## The idea
8: 
9: Most agent demos show the happy path. Ouroboros treats failure as the feature:
10: 
11: 1. **Worker** (`ouro/worker/dossier.py`) — given a company domain, it plans, calls Crustdata tools (identify → enrich → people → web search), and synthesizes a verified company dossier. Every LLM call, tool call, and failure is traced in **neatlogs**.
12: 2. **Supervisor** (`ouro/supervisor/heal.py`) — reads the worker's run log and its *own* neatlogs traces, classifies each failure (429s, missing data, verification gaps), picks a remediation, re-runs, and verifies the fix.
13: 
14: The judges' hard-to-fake evidence — *a run where an action failed, showing what the agent did next* — is the product itself.
15: 
16: ## Docs
17: 
18: - `hackathon.md` — the build log (dated entries, evidence links)
19: - `docs/business-plan.md` — cfo.ai unit economics, pricing, runway (numbers pulled from trace costs)
20: - `docs/demo-script.md` — 3-minute demo narration and recording checklist
21: - `docs/submission.md` — judging-criteria evidence map and pre-submission gates
22: 
23: ## Layout
24: 
25: ```
26: ouro/
27: ├── worker/dossier.py     # dossier agent: plan -> tools -> synthesize -> verify
28: ├── supervisor/heal.py    # trace/run-log reader, failure classifier, remediation
29: ├── tools/crustdata.py    # Crustdata API client (with optional fault injection)
30: ├── state.py              # JSONL run log (state across runs)
31: └── trace.py              # neatlogs init/shutdown
32: ```
33: 
34: ## Setup
35: 
36: ```bash
37: python3 -m venv .venv
38: .venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"
39: cp .env.example .env   # fill in keys
40: ```
41: 
42: Env vars:
43: 
44: | Var | Where from |
45: |---|---|
46: | `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY` | Crustdata dashboard (hackathon promo code `NEATLOGS-OCT2026`) |
47: | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | OpenAI |
48: | `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` | app.neatlogs.com → Settings → API keys → **top** key (Project API key, not the `nlw_` ingest key) |
49: 
50: Optional: `OURO_MODEL` (default `gpt-4o`), `OURO_FAULT_INJECT=1` (deterministic first-call 429 per endpoint, for repeatable demo runs).
51: 
52: ## Usage
53: 
54: ```bash
55: .venv/bin/python -m ouro doctor                      # keys + neatlogs probe + crustdata endpoint access
56: .venv/bin/python -m ouro run crustdata.com           # one dossier (traced)
57: .venv/bin/python -m ouro batch a.com,b.com           # batch, state across runs
58: .venv/bin/python -m ouro runs                        # run log summary
59: .venv/bin/python -m ouro supervise --window-hours 24  # classify failures, remediate, rerun, compare
60: ```
61: 
62: Outputs land in `out/<domain>/<run_id>/` (`dossier.json`, `run.json`); the run log is `state/runs.jsonl`.
63: 
64: ### Offline demo (no keys, no network)
65: 
66: ```bash
67: bash scripts/demo.sh
68: ```
69: 
70: `OURO_MOCK=1` swaps the LLM and Crustdata client for deterministic fakes; `OURO_FAULT_INJECT=1` makes the first call to each endpoint 429, so the demo shows the full loop: baseline failure → supervisor classification → `retry_with_backoff` rerun → healed.
71: 
72: `scripts/trace_costs.py` aggregates `out/**/run.json` into success rate, failure counts, token usage, and durations — the inputs for the cfo.ai unit-economics model.
73: 
74: ## Tests

77: .venv/bin/pytest -q   # offline: state log, fault injection, schema validation
78: ```

# Deterministic offline demo of the full self-healing loop: no API keys, no network.

echo

echo

.venv/bin/python -m ouro watch --once

echo
echo "=== Run log (before -> after -> before -> after) ==="
.venv/bin/python -m ouro runs

echo
echo "=== Cost/throughput summary for the cfo.ai business plan ==="
.venv/bin/python scripts/trace_costs.py

result.output:
### Define plugin dependencies in package.json

Source: https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins

Create a package.json file in the .opencode directory to specify external npm packages. OpenCode automatically runs bun install at startup to resolve these dependencies.

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "shescape": "^2.1.0"
  }
}
```

### Plugins > Use a plugin > From local files

Source: https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins

Place JavaScript or TypeScript files in the plugin directory.

- `.opencode/plugins/` - Project-level plugins
- `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` - Global plugins

Files in these directories are automatically loaded at startup.

--------------------------------

### Plugins > Load order

Source: https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins

Plugins are loaded from all sources and all hooks run in sequence. The load order is:

1. Global config (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`)
2. Project config (`opencode.json`)
3. Global plugin directory (`~/.config/opencode/plugins/`)
4. Project plugin directory (`.opencode/plugins/`)

Duplicate npm packages with the same name and version are loaded once. However, a local plugin and an npm plugin with similar names are both loaded separately.

--------------------------------

### Plugins > How plugins are installed

Source: https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins

**npm plugins** are installed automatically using Bun at startup. Packages and their dependencies are cached in `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/`.

**Local plugins** are loaded directly from the plugin directory. To use external packages, you must create a `package.json` within your config directory (see [Dependencies](#dependencies)), or publish the plugin to npm and [add it to your config](/docs/config#plugins).

--------------------------------

### Create a plugin > Basic structure

Source: https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins

```js title=".opencode/plugins/example.js"
export const MyPlugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {
  console.log("Plugin initialized!")

  return {
    // Hook implementations go here
  }
}
```

The plugin function receives:

- `project`: The current project information.
- `directory`: The current working directory.
- `worktree`: The git worktree path.
- `client`: An opencode SDK client for interacting with the AI.
- `$`: Bun's [shell API](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/shell) for executing commands.

      "final_url": "https://docs.entire.io/guides/configuration/privacy-and-redaction",
      "title": "Privacy and Redaction - Entire",
      "description": "Configure redaction layers, image externalization, telemetry, and checkpoint commit signing.",
      "language": "en",
      "text": "Use this page to configure privacy-related behavior for a repository or for your local machine.
By default, Entire redacts API keys, access tokens, credentialed URLs, database connection strings, and private keys before it writes checkpoint metadata. Secret scanning remains active, but you can choose which pattern scanner Entire uses.
For the threat model, the full list of redaction layers, and what each layer does and does not cover, see Security & Privacy.

##  Start Here If

Use this page to:

* choose secret scanner engines
* add PII or custom redaction rules
* turn on the OpenAI Privacy Filter
* move inline images out of transcripts
* opt in or out of anonymous CLI analytics
* change checkpoint commit signing

##  Settings Reference

Every key below lives under `.entire/settings.json` (shared with the team) or `.entire/settings.local.json` (yours alone), except where noted.


| Setting path | Type | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `redaction.betterleaks.enabled` | boolean | `true` | Run Betterleaks for secret pattern matching. **Project settings only** |
| `redaction.goredact.enabled` | boolean | `false` | Run goredact for secret pattern matching. **Project settings only** |
| `redaction.pii.enabled` | boolean | `false` | Turn on PII redaction |
| `redaction.pii.email` | boolean | `true` when PII is on | Redact email addresses |
| `redaction.pii.phone` | boolean | `true` when PII is on | Redact phone numbers |
| `redaction.pii.address` | boolean | `false` | Redact US street addresses |
| `redaction.pii.custom_patterns` | object | `{}` | Label-to-regex map producing `[REDACTED_<LABEL>]` tokens |
| `redaction.custom_redactions` | object | `{}` | Label-to-regex map producing the bare `REDACTED` token |
| `redaction.externalize_images` | boolean | `false` | Lift inline base64 images into the checkpoint’s `assets/` store |
| `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.enabled` | boolean | `false` | Run OPF at push time |
| `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.categories` | object | `{}` | Which OPF categories to detect. At least one is required when OPF is enabled |
| `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.timeout_seconds` | number | `30` | Per-invocation timeout for the `opf` process |
| `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.prompt_default` | string | `"ask"` | `ask`, `never`, or `always` |
| `redaction.openai_privacy_filter.command` | string | `"opf"` | Path to the `opf` binary. **Read only from an untracked `.entire/settings.local.json`** |
| `telemetry` | boolean | `null` | Anonymous CLI analytics |
| `sign_checkpoint_commits` | boolean | `true` | Sign checkpoint commits with your existing Git key |

##  Secret Scanner Engines

Layer 2 of Entire’s redaction pipeline can run Betterleaks, goredact, or both. Betterleaks runs by default and covers several hundred known secret formats. goredact is off by default and checks a smaller set of provider and contextual token shapes with structural validators such as token length or checksums.

CLI 0.10.2 uses Betterleaks and does not support scanner selection. `v0.10.3-nightly.202608210613.680d64782` first exposes the settings below.

Configure scanner selection in the committed project settings file:

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "betterleaks": {
      "enabled": true
    },
    "goredact": {
      "enabled": false
    }
  }
}
```

Entire reads these keys only from `.entire/settings.json`. It ignores them in `.entire/settings.local.json` and logs a warning because scanner selection affects the checkpoint content shared through the repository.

Keep at least one scanner enabled. Entire refuses to load settings when both `redaction.betterleaks.enabled` and `redaction.goredact.enabled` are `false`.

If goredact is the only active scanner and it fails during a scan, Entire stops the checkpoint write. When both scanners run, Entire can complete the write with Betterleaks coverage if goredact fails. See Redaction Layers for the complete pipeline.

##  PII Redaction

PII redaction is disabled by default. Enable it when checkpoint metadata may include personal information such as email addresses, phone numbers, or addresses.

* Project Settings
* Local Settings
* Custom Patterns

Use project settings when PII redaction should apply to everyone working in the repository.

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "pii": {
      "enabled": true,
      "email": true,
      "phone": true,
      "address": false
    }
  }
}
```

Use local settings when PII redaction should apply only to your machine.

.entire/settings.local.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "pii": {
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

Each label becomes part of the replacement token, uppercased. The pattern below produces `[REDACTED_EMPLOYEE_ID]`.

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "pii": {
      "enabled": true,
      "custom_patterns": {
        "employee_id": "EMP-\\d{6}"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

A pattern that reveals an internal ID format is itself sensitive. Put that one in `.entire/settings.local.json`, which stays out of Git.

See PII redaction for categories, defaults, and limitations.

##  User-Defined Redaction

User-defined redaction lets you redact project-specific strings that Entire’s built-in secret detection may not catch. Patterns use Go RE2 syntax, so lookarounds and backreferences are unavailable.

* Inline Rules
* Rule Packs

Use inline rules for a small number of patterns.

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "custom_redactions": {
      "acme_token": "ACME_TOKEN_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}",
      "internal_id": "INTERNAL_[a-z]{6}_[0-9]{4}"
    }
  }
}
```

Put shared rules in `.entire/settings.json`. Put private rules in `.entire/settings.local.json`. Entries merge per key, so a local rule can override one shared key and leave the rest alone.

Use rule packs for larger reusable sets of redaction rules. Shared packs go in `.entire/redactors/`. Personal packs go in `.entire/redactors/local/`, which `entire enable` keeps gitignored.

.entire/redactors/acme-internal.yaml

```
name: acme-internal
version: 1.0.0
description: Internal ACME service tokens
rules:
  - id: acme-token
    description: Long-lived ACME service tokens
    regex: 'ACME_TOKEN_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}'
    samples:
      - { input: "REDACTED", redacted: true }
      - { input: "ACME_TOKEN_short", redacted: false }
  - id: acme-session
    regex: 'asess_[a-f0-9]{32}'
```

`name` has to match the filename stem. Every pack also needs a `version` and at least one rule carrying an `id` and a `regex`. Entire reads the `.yaml`, `.yml`, and `.json` extensions.

Rules take effect on the next CLI or hook invocation. See User-defined redaction for rule pack behavior, sample self-tests, and validation details.

##  OpenAI Privacy Filter

The OpenAI Privacy Filter is an optional layer that runs a local token-classification model over checkpoints at push time, catching names and other personal data that regex layers miss. It is off by default.

OPF runs on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch backend. Repositories on the ref-based backend, which is the default for repositories enabled with CLI 0.10.0 or later, push without the OPF pass. Check `checkpoints.primary.type` in `.entire/settings.json` before enabling OPF, and see Session Storage to change backends.

###  Install `opf`

```
pip install opf
```

Confirm the binary resolves before you enable the filter, because a missing `opf` aborts your pushes:

```
opf --help
```

###  Enable It

OPF needs at least one category. Enabling the filter with no category selected aborts the push with a configuration error rather than tagging commits as scanned.

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "openai_privacy_filter": {
      "enabled": true,
      "categories": {
        "private_person": true
      },
      "timeout_seconds": 30,
      "prompt_default": "ask"
    }
  }
}
```

###  Categories

Set a category to `true` to detect it. Entire rejects unknown category names when it loads settings, so a typo surfaces immediately instead of silently disabling a category.


| Category | Replacement token | Detects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `private_person` | `[REDACTED_PERSON]` | Person names |
| `private_email` | `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` | Email addresses |
| `private_phone` | `[REDACTED_PHONE]` | Phone numbers |
| `private_address` | `[REDACTED_ADDRESS]` | Street addresses |
| `private_url` | `[REDACTED_URL]` | URLs that may identify a person or account |
| `private_date` | `[REDACTED_DATE]` | Dates such as a date of birth |
| `account_number` | `[REDACTED_ACCOUNT_NUMBER]` | Account, card, and SSN-shaped numbers |
| `secret` | `REDACTED` | Generic credential-shaped values |

###  Control the Pre-Push Prompt

`prompt_default` decides whether the pre-push hook asks before running OPF.


| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `"ask"` | Prompt on an interactive push. This is the default |
| `"always"` | Run without asking |
| `"never"` | Skip OPF, and push content redacted by the regex layers only |

Choosing **Always** at the prompt writes `prompt_default: "always"` into `.entire/settings.local.json` for you.

###  Override for a Single Push

`ENTIRE_OPF` beats both the setting and the prompt, for that push only.

```
ENTIRE_OPF=no git push
```

Use `ENTIRE_OPF=no` when a CI runner pushes without `opf` installed. Use `ENTIRE_OPF=yes` to run OPF without a prompt.

###  Push Caps

Two environment variables bound how much work one push hands to the model. Both accept a number or `unlimited`.


| Variable | Default | Guards against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ENTIRE_OPF_BOOTSTRAP_LIMIT` | `100` commits | A first push to a remote with no checkpoint history rewriting hours of commits |
| `ENTIRE_OPF_BATCH_LIMIT` | `2097152` bytes (2 MiB) | A single commit carrying a very large pasted transcript |

```
ENTIRE_OPF_BATCH_LIMIT=10485760 git push
```

###  The `command` Setting

`command` points at a specific `opf` binary. Entire reads it only from `.entire/settings.local.json`, and only when that file is untracked, because the value becomes a process Entire executes during `git push`. Entire logs a rejected `command` and falls back to `$PATH`.

.entire/settings.local.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "openai_privacy_filter": {
      "command": "/opt/homebrew/bin/opf"
    }
  }
}
```

See The `command` setting is local-only for why this restriction exists.

##  Externalized Images

`redaction.externalize_images` moves inline base64 images out of transcript files and into the checkpoint’s `assets/` store, replacing each with a short `entire-asset:assets/...` placeholder. It is off by default.

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "redaction": {
    "externalize_images": true
  }
}
```

`ENTIRE_EXTERNALIZE_IMAGES=1` turns it on for one invocation without editing settings.
Turning this on keeps large binary blobs out of `full.jsonl` and `transcript.jsonl`, which makes those files cheaper to read and diff. Restore re-injects images byte-exactly whether or not the flag is on.

This setting changes where Entire stores image bytes, not whether any layer scans them. No redaction layer reads image content in either arrangement, so an image containing a credential or customer data reaches the remote intact. See Externalized images.

##  Telemetry

Telemetry controls anonymous CLI usage analytics. It does not send prompts, transcripts, source code, file paths, repository names, or flag values.

* Settings File
* Environment Variable

To opt out in this repository, set:

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "telemetry": false
}
```

Use `.entire/settings.local.json` instead when the telemetry preference should apply only to your machine.

To opt out for a single command or shell environment, set:

```
ENTIRE_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1 entire status
```

See Telemetry and analytics for what is and is not captured.

##  Checkpoint Commit Signing

Checkpoint commits are signed by default when your Git signing setup is available.
To disable signing for the repository, set:

.entire/settings.json

```
{
  "sign_checkpoint_commits": false
}
```

Use `.entire/settings.local.json` instead when the signing preference should apply only to your machine.
See Checkpoint commit signing for requirements and best-effort behavior.

##  Verify Privacy Settings

After changing privacy settings, run:

```
entire status --detailed
```

For redaction changes, run a normal Entire workflow after updating settings. Entire skips an invalid regex or a malformed rule pack and writes the reason to `.entire/logs/entire.log` instead of stopping the CLI.
To confirm OPF ran, push and then check the checkpoint commit for its trailer:

```
git log -1 --format=%B entire/checkpoints/v1 | grep Entire-OPF-Applied

### Later on Day 1: watch daemon + failure-kind hardening

- Watch daemon (`ouro watch --once` / `--interval N`): polls the run log, heals each *new* failure exactly once, tracks state in `state/watch_state.json`. Verified via CLI: seeded failure → cycle 1 healed it → cycle 2 healed nothing (dedup confirmed).

### Later on Day 1: Entire checkpoint capture (root cause)

- Symptom: `entire session list` empty and `entire checkpoint list` shows 0 after every commit.
- Cause: the Entire opencode plugin lives at `.opencode/plugins/entire.ts` inside this repo, but the opencode session driving the build runs with project root `/Users/sathwik` (home), so the plugin never loads and no session hooks fire. Git hooks work; session capture does not.
- Fix for future sessions: launch opencode from inside the repo (`cd ~/ouroboros && opencode`) so the plugin loads and checkpoints attach automatically.
- For this session: attach manually via `entire session attach <session-id> --agent opencode`.
- Safety gate: an earlier debug command printed a TinyFish API key into this session's transcript. Before any attach is pushed, redaction rules in `.entire/settings.local.json` (untracked) must strip it, verified by grepping the checkpoint ref for the key prefix. `strategy_options.push_sessions` is also `false` so raw session logs never auto-push.
